name: Anglican Churches: Beginnings and Splits
summary: How the Church of England broke from Rome under Henry VIII, took shape under Edward VI and Elizabeth I, spread as a worldwide communion, and divided over Puritanism, Methodism, churchmanship, and sexuality.

start.label: Act of Supremacy makes Henry VIII supreme head of the Church of England

end.label: Global South Anglicans reject the Archbishop of Canterbury's leadership after the Church of England allows blessings of same-sex couples

key_dates.label: Cranmer's first Book of Common Prayer
Thirty-Nine Articles made binding on clergy
Great Ejection of about 2,000 Puritan ministers
Protestant Episcopal Church organized in the United States
First Lambeth Conference of Anglican bishops
Reformed Episcopal Church separates from the Episcopal Church
Continuing Anglican churches form at the Congress of St. Louis
Church of England votes to ordain women as priests
Episcopal Church consecrates Gene Robinson, an openly gay bishop
Anglican Church in North America founded, after GAFCON (2008)

background.text: Henry VIII broke with Rome after Pope Clement VII refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon; the break was political at first, with Catholic doctrine largely kept until Henry's death.

happened.text: Under Edward VI, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer introduced Protestant worship in English through the Book of Common Prayer; Mary I restored Catholicism (1553–58); Elizabeth I settled a Protestant church with bishops and traditional forms.
Puritans who wanted further reform were pushed out after the Restoration (1662) and formed the Nonconformist churches; Methodists separated after Wesley's death.
The church spread with the British Empire and missions, forming the Anglican Communion of independent provinces linked to the Archbishop of Canterbury.
From the 1970s disputes over women's ordination and sexuality led to breakaway churches and a split between conservative provinces, mostly in the Global South, and Western provinces.

participants.name: Thomas Cranmer
participants.role: Archbishop who wrote the Book of Common Prayer

participants.name: Thomas More
participants.role: Executed for refusing to accept the royal supremacy

participants.name: John Wesley
participants.role: Anglican priest whose movement became Methodism

outcomes.text: The Anglican Communion has tens of millions of members, the largest share in Africa, but is divided over authority and sexuality.

condemnations.reason: Elizabeth I excommunicated and declared deposed, releasing her subjects from obedience
Anglican ordinations declared 'absolutely null and utterly void'

persecution_note: The English Reformation brought executions on all sides as the official religion changed with each monarch.

persecution.title: Executions under Henry VIII
persecution.summary: Those who refused the oath acknowledging the royal supremacy were executed, including Bishop John Fisher, Thomas More, and Carthusian monks of London (1535); Henry also burned Protestants who denied Catholic doctrines.

responsible.name: Thomas Cromwell
responsible.role: Chief minister who enforced the supremacy

persecution.title: Burnings under Mary I
persecution.summary: About 280 Protestants, including Archbishop Cranmer and Bishops Latimer and Ridley, were burned for heresy.
persecution.outcome: Remembered through Foxe's Book of Martyrs.

persecution.title: Executions of Catholics under Elizabeth I
persecution.summary: After the papal excommunication of Elizabeth, Catholic priests were treated as traitors; about 180–200 Catholics, most of them priests such as Edmund Campion (1581), were executed.

responsible.name: Francis Walsingham and William Cecil
responsible.role: Ministers who ran the campaign against Catholic priests

persecution.outcome: Many later canonized by the Catholic Church.
